Stalk
STAWK
noun
From the Saxon staelc, akin to stele, a stem or handle; hence the standing stem of a plant which bears the ear — that without which the grain has nothing to grow on and nothing to grow from.

Biblical Definition

The stalk is the standing stem that carries the ear of corn. Scripture uses it in three places, and each is weighty. In Pharaoh’s second dream, “seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good” (Gen 41:5), and Pharaoh repeats it to Joseph — “seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good” (Gen 41:22). One stalk bearing seven full ears is superabundance; the seven thin ears blasted with the east wind that swallowed them are the famine that no plenty could withstand, and Joseph tells Pharaoh that the doubling of the dream means “the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.” In Joshua, Rahab hides the spies under the stalks of flax laid in order upon her roof (Jos 2:6) — a woman of Jericho covering the covenant people with the ordinary produce of her house, and finding mercy in the day the city fell. And in Hosea comes the sentence that governs the whole theme: “For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal” (Hos 8:7). Israel’s religion had greenness without substance. Something came up; nothing came of it. A crop with no stalk cannot stand, and a bud with no meal cannot feed, and what the strangers do not swallow the whirlwind takes.

Webster 1828 Definition

The stem of a plant which bears the ear; in Hosea the emblem of a religion that shows growth but yields no meal.

STALK, the stem or main axis of a plant, which supports the leaves, flower, and fruit.

From the Saxon staelc; kindred with stele, a stem or handle.

Hebrew qaneh, a reed or stem (Gen 41:5), and qamah, standing corn (Hos 8:7).

Jos 2:6 uses the plural of flax stalks, laid in order upon a roof to dry.

Hos 8:7 — “it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal”: growth without substance.

Key Scripture

Gen 41:5 — "And he slept and dreamed the second time: and, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good."

Gen 41:22 — "And I saw in my dream, and, behold, seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good:"

Hos 8:7 — "For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up."

Jos 2:6 — "But she had brought them up to the roof of the house, and hid them with the stalks of flax, which she had laid in order upon the roof."

Modern Corruption

Hosea’s diagnosis is inverted. Visible growth is taken for proof of life, and a religion that shows leaf but yields no meal is counted a harvest because it looks green.

expand to see more

Hosea 8 describes a nation full of religious activity: kings set up, altars multiplied, calves cast, offerings brought. By any count of visible growth Israel was thriving. God’s verdict is that the crop has no stalk. The wind they sowed — their alliances, their innovations in worship, their borrowed gods — comes back as a whirlwind, and the bud that promised meal yields none. The error that stalks this word is the counting of buds. Where numbers, energy, and the appearance of growth are taken as the measure, a movement can be enormous and have no stalk in it: nothing that will stand when the wind rises, nothing that will feed a hungry soul. Our Lord walked the same field. Some seed sprang up quickly in stony ground, and the very speed of it was the symptom — because it had no deepness of earth, it withered when the sun was up. The remedy is not to despise growth but to ask Hosea’s question of it: is there a stalk? Will it stand? Is there meal in the bud?

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives the increase, and He gives it through means He has appointed rather than the means men invent. Pharaoh’s good stalk bore seven ears because God set them there; the doubled dream meant the thing was established by God. Hosea’s Israel had ears enough to look at and no stalk under them because they had sown the wind. Between those two stands the ordinary Christian labour of sowing what God actually commanded — the preached word, the ordinances, prayer, the plain duties of the household — and waiting on Him for the ear. “Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7) cuts both ways, and it cuts with particular sharpness against a church that would rather sow the wind and count the buds than sow the word and wait for the meal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The stem that bears the ear; the difference between a crop that will stand and a greenness that yields nothing.

expand to see more

Stalk — Saxon staelc, akin to stele, a stem.

Gen 41:5, 22 — seven full ears on one stalk, the sign of Egypt’s seven plenteous years.

The doubling of Pharaoh’s dream meant, in Joseph’s words, that the thing was established by God.

Jos 2:6 — Rahab hides the spies under stalks of flax laid in order on her roof.

Hos 8:7 — sown wind, reaped whirlwind: no stalk, and the bud yields no meal.

Usage

"One stalk bearing seven full ears is plenty; seven thin ears swallowing them is famine God has established."

"Hosea’s charge is growth without substance: something came up, nothing came of it."

"Ask of any movement what Hosea asked of Israel — is there a stalk, and is there meal in the bud?"
